title: Massive New Study Shows How Young People Feel About AI Companions
content:
A new study from Gallup looked at how young people across the world are making friends, both digitally and in person. The good news is that around 93% of the young people surveyed reported having at least one strong in-person friendship. The weird news is that 33% said they had an AI companion.

Gallup’s study is lengthy and nuanced. It partnered with the Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab to conduct the study and used online surveys of more than 16,000 young people from the ages of 15 to 22 in 16 different countries.

A lot of the topline results won’t surprise anyone living in today’s constantly online digital-forward age. Gallup found that respondents felt their in-person friendships were their strongest, that digital friendships complemented rather than replaced in-person ones, and that stronger friendships made people happier no matter how the connection was made. Three things that stood out were how the young respondents talked about AI, loneliness, and doomscrolling.

title: BREAKING: Everything
content: A few hours ago, I went to rent a Lime bike to ride the ten minutes to my therapy appointment. I opened Lime, scanned the QR code, and double clicked my iPhone’s side button to authorize Apple Pay. The app hung for a few moments, then closed. I tried several more times and the same thing happened. In the back of my mind, I wondered what was going on — was the Lime bike broken? Was my cell phone service out? Was it something else? I opened the Uber app and, similarly, wasn’t able to pay. I opened DownDetector and realized that the entirety of Apple Pay, a thing I thought existed only on my phone and not the cloud, was down. I texted my therapist, put my phone in my pocket, and started jogging.

title: A Man and His Muse AI Agent Sue Meta
content: In his 6,500-word manifesto earlier this year, Mark Zuckerberg said people would use Meta’s AI agents to “work 24/7 on your behalf to improve your relationships, health, career, finances, home management, hobbies, and more.” Just a few months after that pronouncement, a man in South Carolina named Joe Thomas has used Meta’s Muse agent to sue Meta after the company’s content moderation filters locked his epoxy countertop business’s Facebook page after he gave his agent, “Baby Mia,” access to the account.

title: Lakes Are Bizarrely Syncing Up Globally, And Scientists Are Worried
content:
Lakes around the world have become increasingly synced up in their ecological conditions—such as warming temperatures, algal blooms, and oxygen levels—a trend that reveals “a possible fundamental reorganization of the world’s lake systems,” according to a study published on Monday in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 

Lakes come in all kinds of shapes, sizes, and volumes, and vary widely in other critical properties, such as temperature, composition, and biomass. This diversity of lake conditions, known as spatial heterogeneity, serves as a handy buffer against environmental disruptions; because each lake responds to events differently, they curb the spread of potential damage.

But when scientists studied satellite imagery of roughly 2,000 lakes around the world since the year 2000, they discovered that lakes “are undergoing a profound shift toward spatial synchrony through time” that “strongly indicates that increasing lake synchrony is a genuine, global-scale phenomenon,“ according to the study.

title: 'Defense by ChatGPT'
content:
We've written a lot about how AI generated writing has collided with – and created chaos for – the legal system in the last few years, from lawyers using it to do their research and filings for them to judges getting extremely fed up with dealing with these attorneys. In some cases, judges have sanctioned offending attorneys thousands of dollars for using AI to do their jobs, and lawyers give endless excuses when they're busted, with some calling it a “cautionary tale." Today's story is about how the DOJ is getting involved: by trying to catch attorneys doing "defense by ChatGPT."

Lawyers for the Department of Justice are using the AI writing detection service Pangram to argue that opposing attorneys are using AI to write legal arguments, and in one case told the court that opposing counsel was doing “defense by ChatGPT,” and writing “AI slop” filings, according to court filings reviewed by 404 Media.

title: The Department of Justice Is Using AI Detector Pangram Against Defense Attorneys
content:
Lawyers for the Department of Justice are using the AI writing detection service Pangram to argue that opposing attorneys are using AI to write legal arguments, and in one case told the court that opposing counsel was doing “defense by ChatGPT,” and writing “AI slop” filings, according to court filings reviewed by 404 Media. 

Over the last few years, we have documented many attorneys getting caught by judges using AI after citing hallucinated cases that do not exist. The filings in this court case over the past month show attorneys, including those working for the government, are trying to catch each other using AI, then are citing their opponents’ AI use in their arguments to the court.

title: How an AI Content Mill Put a Real Musician Through Copyright Hell
content:
When writer and musician Samantha Shokin noticed her cover of a public domain Bulgarian folk song had been copyright struck on YouTube, she assumed it would be easy to fix. It wasn’t. And trying to figure out what happened led her to discover an AI content mill that is running 500 slop-filled channels and abusing YouTube’s automated copyright detectors.

“Any human would agree with me that there’s something clearly wrong here that needs to be fixed, but I can’t get in touch with a human being,” Shokin said.

Shokin’s journey is a modern nightmare that highlights the ways AI can be weaponized against human creators, and the ways people fall through the cracks of big tech’s automated systems.

During the pandemic, Shokin recorded a 50 second version of the Bulgarian folk song ‘Bre Petrunko’ and uploaded it to SoundCloud, where it didn’t get much traction. Two years later, she uploaded it to YouTube and watched as her cover grew in popularity, gaining 125,000 views in four years.

title: This Comic Kills Technofascists
content:
Dave Maass has been writing about comics for more than 20 years, and now he also writes comics. By day, he teaches tech investigative techniques at the University of Nevada, Reno Reynolds School of Journalism and researches surveillance at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. 

If I was the manager of a comic book store, I’d create a section for “journalism nerdcore.” It’s where I would stock Transmetropolitan, DMZ, and Abbott–comics that place fictional journalists in the center of genre stories, be it science fiction, action or horror. Despite their daylight jobs, Spider-Man and Superman wouldn’t be allowed there, but DC’s Lois Lane would find a home of her own. 

On the end-of-shelf display, with a big fat, Sharpie-written “Employee Pick of 2026” sign: Exploit, the new comic series from Laura Hudson and Tim Leong and illustrator Emiliana Pinna, which was just published last month by Mad Cave Studios in its collected trade paperback volume. It doesn’t get more journalism nerdcore than its tag line: “Don’t Bury The Lede. Bury Your Enemies!”

title: Scientists Made Monkeys Watch Minions to Study Their Brains
content:
Welcome back to the Abstract! These are the studies this week that watched movies, made sacrifices, got crafty, and aged backwards.

First, scientists learn how primates make meaning out of visuals by peeking into the brains of monkeys as they watch Despicable Me. Then: human sacrifice as climate “crisis rituals,” the fingerprints of prehistoric children, and the longevity secrets of ants.

As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files. 

Raghavan, Vinay S et al. “During natural vision, semantic novelty modulates fixation-related processing in primate cortex.” JNeurosci.

Settling down to watch a film is often viewed as a way to relax and shut our brains off for a while. Our brains, however, beg to differ—they are as busy as ever when interpreting videos, according to a new study based on brainwaves of humans and primates as they watch movies and short clips.

title: High-End Furniture Marketplace AptDeco Is Taking People’s Furniture and Not Paying Them
content:
Last month, Erin sold a $3,000 large designer table on AptDeco, a white glove high-end furniture marketplace. More than a month later, she feels like she’s been literally robbed.

“AptDeco sent three men to physically collect my table on October 13, and here we are on November 16, with no payment and no concrete explanation for where my $2,000 (after their absurd $900 fee) is,” Erin told me. “It genuinely feels like I’ve had something stolen from me.”

AptDeco is a Y Combinator-backed company whose entire purpose is to take the risk out of places like Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist for designer furniture resale. It advertises itself as “simple and seamless,” and says “we handle pickup, delivery, and payments,” and claims that it pays sellers “within 5-10 business days.” But over the last few months, people who have sold furniture on the platform say that AptDeco has sold their furniture and taken it from their houses, but hasn’t paid them. 404 Media agreed to only use Erin’s first name because she is still trying to get her money from the company.

title: Black Neighborhoods Are Twice as Likely To House a Data Center, Study Finds
content:
Developers build data centers in communities of color at more than twice the rate they do in white neighborhoods, according to a new study from researchers at George Washington University and the Center for Security, Innovation & New Technology (CSINT) at American University.

According to the study, “Redlining in the Age of AI: The Relationship between Data Center Locations and Race in the US” majority-Black neighborhoods have 2.2 times the odds of hosting a data center than a white neighborhood in the same state. The number goes up to 2.6 in majority-Hispanic neighborhoods and 4.2 times in majority-Asian neighborhoods. “As the share of Black, Hispanic, and Asian residents in a neighborhood increases, so do the odds that the neighborhood hosts a data center,” the researchers wrote.

title: ICE Is Paying AT&T to Dig Through a Mountain of Call Records
content:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement is paying telecommunications giant AT&T millions of dollars to have AT&T’s analysts sift through mountains of raw AT&T data for a wide variety of investigations, according to an internal ICE document obtained by 404 Media, other procurement records, and experts who reviewed those records. Civil liberty experts have called it a mass surveillance program, and they say the data can include trillions of phone records and location data. 

The AT&T product, interchangeably called Data Analytics and Support Services or Data Analytical Services, appears to be related to an earlier surveillance program called Hemisphere, in which AT&T provided U.S. authorities at state, local, and federal levels access to AT&T user data. Though that program shut down, ICE is still paying for access to raw data under this new arrangement with AT&T, according to the restricted ICE procurement document obtained by 404 Media. The program likely affects more than just AT&T customers because the company connects phone calls for other phone companies, meaning non-customers are likely swept up too, according to a surveillance expert.

title: Charting American Culture in News Footage of ‘Grand Theft Auto’
content:
Some people spent the week leading up to the release of Grand Theft Auto VI replaying the old games. I, sicko that I am, spent it watching TV news coverage of the franchise from the past 20 years.

Grand Theft Auto has been a staple of cable and broadcast TV news since at least the release of Grand Theft Auto III in 2001. I’ve been an adult for all of it; I’ve had a front row seat for two decades of moral panics, parental freakouts, and bizarre political theater. The games and the broader culture’s reaction to them have changed dramatically in that time. In 2001, newscasters worried GTA III was training an army of young men to kill. In 2026, The New York Times earnestly quoted Bell Hooks in its review of GTA VI.

For mainstream news, GTA is the ur-video game. The open world that mirrors our own, the prevalence of sex and death, and the increasingly realistic simulations and graphics pointed towards the dream of what a video game could be. GTA is the American id made manifest.

title: The AI in ‘Musk’ Is Cringe
content:
Three hours and 15 minutes into the 4 hour long documentary Musk, a video game avatar of the titular billionaire picks up a chainsaw off the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office. Shot like a first-person shooter, the audience watches as Musk wields the chainsaw to destroy various government buildings. Walking through a farm, Musk aims the chainsaw at grain silos labeled ‘USDA’ and lightning arcs from its spinning blades. The silo explodes and cows moo in distress.

In my experience, the purpose of a video game chainsaw is to viscerally rend through objects. I have never seen one shoot lightning. It’s a small detail that speaks to my overall problem with Alex Gibney’s Musk: it’s cringe.

Elon Musk is one of the most powerful men alive on the planet and Gibney’s Musk does a decent job of giving the overall arc of the man’s many faults. The director takes us from Zip2 to DOGE while highlighting the billionaire’s pathology, and it hits more than it misses.
